Will this booking
be cancelled?

A classifier that flags risky hotel bookings using only what is known at booking time — and a close look at two evaluation traps that make scores look far better than they are.

Notebook on GitHub ↗ PDF report ↗ Video on YouTubecoming soon
119,390bookings × 32 columns
27.8%duplicate rows found and removed
0.708test F1 (Logistic Regression baseline 0.580)
0.898test ROC-AUC (baseline 0.853)

The problem

More than a third of the bookings in this dataset are cancelled. A hotel that sees cancellations coming can overbook in a controlled way, ask guests to reconfirm, or require a deposit.

We predict is_canceled from booking-time attributes — lead time, sales channel, deposit type, price, special requests, guest history — compare five models, handle the class imbalance, and pick a decision threshold that balances missed cancellations against false alarms.

The dataset

Source
Hotel Booking Demand — Antonio, Almeida & Nunes, Data in Brief (2019), CC BY 4.0
Size
119,390 bookings × 32 columns, two hotels in Portugal, arrivals Jul 2015 – Aug 2017
Target
is_canceled — 37.0% raw, 27.6% after removing duplicates
Challenges
missing values (company 94%, agent 14%, hidden Undefined), 27.8% duplicates, target leakage, outliers (ADR up to 5,400), class imbalance

1. Dataset description¶

Hotel Booking Demand (Antonio, Almeida & Nunes, Data in Brief, 2019; CC BY 4.0) contains real bookings from two hotels in Portugal — a City Hotel in Lisbon and a Resort Hotel in the Algarve — with arrival dates between July 2015 and August 2017. Each row is one booking.

Group Columns Meaning
Target is_canceled 1 if the booking was cancelled
Timing lead_time, arrival_date_* days between booking and arrival; arrival year/month/week/day
Stay stays_in_weekend_nights, stays_in_week_nights, adults, children, babies number of nights and guests
Channel & guest market_segment, distribution_channel, customer_type, country, agent, company, is_repeated_guest booking source, customer type, nationality
History previous_cancellations, previous_bookings_not_canceled the guest's past cancellations / completed stays
Service & price meal, reserved_room_type, deposit_type, adr, required_car_parking_spaces, total_of_special_requests, booking_changes, days_in_waiting_list meal plan, room type, deposit, average daily rate (ADR)
Leakage reservation_status, reservation_status_date, assigned_room_type only known after the guest arrives or cancels → must not be used

2. Data quality & EDA¶

2.1 Missing values — visible and hidden¶

Besides NaN, the dataset encodes missing values with the string "Undefined" (according to the original documentation, meal = Undefined is equivalent to SC — no meal package).

In [5]:
hidden = {c: int((raw[c] == "Undefined").sum()) for c in raw.select_dtypes("object") if (raw[c] == "Undefined").any()}
missing = pd.DataFrame({
    "NaN": raw.isna().sum(),
    "Undefined": pd.Series(hidden),
}).fillna(0).astype(int)
missing = missing[(missing.sum(axis=1) > 0)].sort_values("NaN", ascending=False)
missing["%"] = (missing.sum(axis=1) / len(raw) * 100).round(2)

Observation. company is 94% missing — but here "missing" is not an error, it means "not booked through a company". Likewise, a missing agent (13.7%) means "booked directly by the guest". So instead of dropping these rows, we turn the two columns into binary flags has_company, has_agent. country (0.4%) and children (4 rows) are imputed with the most frequent value / median inside the pipeline.

rows

Bookings with 0 guests 180

  • 27% of rows are duplicates — mostly group bookings entered many times with identical details. If kept, the same record can land in both train and test and inflate the scores (section 4.3 measures by how much).
  • 180 bookings with 0 guests, 1 booking with negative ADR and 1 booking with ADR = 5400 (~50× the median) are entry errors → removed.
  • 0-night bookings (day use) are valid from a business perspective → kept.

A 63/37 split — moderately imbalanced. A model that always predicts "not cancelled" already reaches ~63% accuracy while catching zero cancellations, so we focus on F1, recall, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC rather than accuracy.

Cancellation rate by deposit_type:
 deposit_type
No Deposit    0.284
Non Refund    0.994
Refundable    0.222

Lead time 0–7 days: 9.6%  |  >365 days: 67.7%
0 special requests: 47.7%  |  3+ requests: 16.8%

Findings (figure 2.4).

  • Lead time: the earlier the booking, the more likely the cancellation — 9.6% for bookings made ≤ 7 days ahead vs 67.7% for bookings made more than a year ahead. Guests have more time to change their plans.
  • Non Refund bookings are cancelled 99% of the time — counter-intuitive (the guest paid a non-refundable price and still cancelled). This is a known quirk of the dataset: most of these rows are group/agency block bookings (Groups, Offline TA/TO) that were cancelled en masse. Section 3.1 shows that most of them are duplicates.
  • Groups have the highest cancellation rate (61%); Direct/Corporate the lowest (15–19%).
  • Guests with special requests (high floor, twin beds…) cancel far less (48% → 17%) — they have already "invested" in the trip.

def iqr_outliers(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return ((s < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum()

num_cols_raw = ["lead_time", "adr", "stays_in_week_nights", "stays_in_weekend_nights", "days_in_waiting_list",

    "IQR outliers": [iqr_outliers(raw[c]) for c in num_cols_raw],
    "skewness": [raw[c].skew() for c in num_cols_raw],
    "max": [raw[c].max() for c in num_cols_raw],

The numerical columns are strongly right-skewed (skewness > 1) and have thousands of points beyond the IQR fences. Most of them are real values (bookings made two years ahead, expensive suites), so we do not delete them. Instead we winsorize (clip to the 0.5%–99.5% quantiles learned on the training set) and, for count/day columns, apply log1p to reduce skew before scaling. Only obvious errors (negative ADR, ADR = 5400, 0 guests) are removed.

Correlations with the target are weak to moderate (|ρ| ≤ 0.32): lead_time (+0.32) and previous_cancellations (+0.27) are positive, total_of_special_requests (−0.26) and required_car_parking_spaces (−0.20) negative. No single numerical feature decides the outcome → we need a model that combines many features, including categorical ones (deposit_type, market_segment, country).

3. Data preparation¶

3.1 Row-level cleaning¶

These steps do not learn any parameter from the data, so doing them before the split does not leak information.

In [13]:
class HotelDataCleaner:
    """Row-level cleaning: drop leakage columns, invalid bookings and duplicates."""

    def __init__(self, leak_cols, drop_duplicates=True):
        self.leak_cols = leak_cols
        self.drop_duplicates = drop_duplicates
        self.log = []

    def _step(self, df, mask, reason):
        self.log.append((reason, int(mask.sum())))
        return df.loc[~mask]

    def clean(self, df):
        df = df.drop(columns=self.leak_cols).copy()
        guests = df["adults"] + df["children"].fillna(0) + df["babies"]
        df = self._step(df, guests == 0, "0 guests")
        df = self._step(df, (df["adr"] < 0) | (df["adr"] > 1000), "ADR negative or > 1000")
        if self.drop_duplicates:
            df = self._step(df, df.duplicated(), "duplicate")
        # "Undefined" is a missing marker; per dataset docs meal Undefined == SC
        df["meal"] = df["meal"].replace("Undefined", "SC")
        for c in ["market_segment", "distribution_channel"]:
            df[c] = df[c].replace("Undefined", np.nan)
        return df.reset_index(drop=True)

    def report(self):
        return pd.DataFrame(self.log, columns=["reason", "rows removed"])


cleaner = HotelDataCleaner(LEAK_COLS)
df = cleaner.clean(raw)
display(cleaner.report())
print(f"Kept {len(df):,} / {len(raw):,} rows ({len(df) / len(raw):.1%}); new cancellation rate: {df['is_canceled'].mean():.1%}")
nr_before, nr_after = (raw["deposit_type"] == "Non Refund").sum(), (df["deposit_type"] == "Non Refund").sum()
print(f"'Non Refund' bookings: {nr_before:,} → {nr_after:,} ({1 - nr_after / nr_before:.0%} were duplicates)")

0 0 guests 180

Kept 85,982 / 119,390 rows (72.0%); new cancellation rate: 27.6%
'Non Refund' bookings: 14,587 → 1,010 (93% were duplicates)

After removing duplicates the cancellation rate drops from 37.0% to 27.6%: most duplicated records were cancelled group bookings — in particular 93% of Non Refund bookings were copies (14,587 → 1,010). The clean data is therefore more imbalanced (72.4/27.6), and the "Non Refund → cancelled" pattern from section 2.4 comes mostly from duplicated rows.

3.2 Feature engineering (HotelFeatureBuilder class)¶

New features with business meaning, written as a scikit-learn transformer so they live inside the pipeline:

  • total_nights, total_guests, has_children, is_weekend_only
  • has_agent, has_company (replacing the two mostly-missing ID columns)
  • is_domestic (Portuguese guests), arrival_weekday
  • month_sin, month_cos: cyclical encoding of the month (December is next to January)
In [14]:
MONTHS = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August",
          "September", "October", "November", "December"]


class HotelFeatureBuilder(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Stateless feature engineering applied inside the sklearn pipeline."""

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        X = X.copy()
        month = X["arrival_date_month"].map({m: i + 1 for i, m in enumerate(MONTHS)})
        X["total_nights"] = X["stays_in_weekend_nights"] + X["stays_in_week_nights"]
        X["total_guests"] = X["adults"] + X["children"].fillna(0) + X["babies"]
        X["has_children"] = ((X["children"].fillna(0) + X["babies"]) > 0).astype(int)
        X["is_weekend_only"] = ((X["stays_in_week_nights"] == 0) & (X["stays_in_weekend_nights"] > 0)).astype(int)
        X["has_agent"] = X["agent"].notna().astype(int)
        X["has_company"] = X["company"].notna().astype(int)
        X["is_domestic"] = (X["country"] == "PRT").astype(int)
        # errors="coerce": permuted/unseen inputs can form invalid dates (e.g. 29 Feb 2017) -> weekday -1
        arrival = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=X["arrival_date_year"], month=month, day=X["arrival_date_day_of_month"]),
                                 errors="coerce")
        X["arrival_weekday"] = arrival.dt.dayofweek.fillna(-1)
        X["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * month / 12)
        X["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * month / 12)
        return X.drop(columns=["agent", "company", "arrival_date_month", "arrival_date_year"])

3.3 Train / validation / test split¶

A 70 / 15 / 15 split, stratified on the target. The validation set is used to compare models, tune hyperparameters and pick the decision threshold; the test set is used once, at the very end.

3.4 Preprocessing pipeline: imputation → outliers → encoding → scaling¶

Every learned parameter (medians, winsorizing quantiles, means/stds, one-hot categories) is fit on the training set only through Pipeline + ColumnTransformer, so no information leaks from validation/test.

Group Columns Processing
Right-skewed counts/days lead_time, total_nights, days_in_waiting_list, previous_cancellations, … median impute → Winsorizer (0.5–99.5%) → log1p → StandardScaler
Price adr median impute → Winsorizer → StandardScaler (no log: 1.6% of adr values are 0 — complimentary rooms — and log1p would split them into a far-away cluster, turning skew from 0.88 into −3.6)
Other numerical adults, total_guests, month_sin, … median impute → StandardScaler
Categorical hotel, meal, market_segment, deposit_type, country, … most-frequent impute → OneHotEncoder (categories below 0.5% merged into infrequent)
In [16]:
class Winsorizer(OneToOneFeatureMixin, BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Clip each column to [q_low, q_high] quantiles learned on the training data."""

    def __init__(self, q_low=0.005, q_high=0.995):
        self.q_low = q_low
        self.q_high = q_high

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        self.n_features_in_ = X.shape[1]
        self.low_ = np.nanquantile(X, self.q_low, axis=0)
        self.high_ = np.nanquantile(X, self.q_high, axis=0)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.low_, self.high_)


SKEWED = ["lead_time", "total_nights", "stays_in_weekend_nights", "stays_in_week_nights",
          "days_in_waiting_list", "previous_cancellations", "previous_bookings_not_canceled", "booking_changes"]
WINSOR_ONLY = ["adr"]
OTHER_NUM = ["adults", "children", "babies", "total_guests", "required_car_parking_spaces",
             "total_of_special_requests", "arrival_date_week_number", "arrival_date_day_of_month",
             "arrival_weekday", "month_sin", "month_cos", "is_repeated_guest", "has_children",
             "is_weekend_only", "has_agent", "has_company", "is_domestic"]
CATEGORICAL = ["hotel", "meal", "country", "market_segment", "distribution_channel",
               "reserved_room_type", "deposit_type", "customer_type"]


def make_preprocessor():
    skewed_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("winsor", Winsorizer()),
        ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")),
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ])
    winsor_pipe = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("winsor", Winsorizer()), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    num_pipe = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    cat_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=0.005, sparse_output=False)),
    ])
    pre = ColumnTransformer([("skewed", skewed_pipe, SKEWED), ("winsor", winsor_pipe, WINSOR_ONLY),
                             ("num", num_pipe, OTHER_NUM), ("cat", cat_pipe, CATEGORICAL)])
    return Pipeline([("features", HotelFeatureBuilder()), ("columns", pre)])

Xt_train = prep.transform(X_train)

print("Example one-hot country columns:", [f for f in feature_names if f.startswith("cat__country")][:8], "...")

Finding (figure 3.4). After preprocessing both columns have mean ≈ 0 and std ≈ 1. The skew of lead_time drops from 1.43 to |−0.71| and that of adr from 0.88 to 0.76 (winsorizing trims the right tail). In our first version we also applied log1p to adr and its skew got worse (−3.6) — which is why adr has its own branch. Scaling matters for Logistic Regression (sensitive to feature scale and extreme values); tree models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) are essentially unaffected, but we use the same pipeline everywhere for a fair comparison.

4. Modelling & comparison¶

4.1 The ModelBenchmark class¶

A small class that trains several models on the same preprocessing pipeline, computes the same metrics and stores the results.

In [18]:
class ModelBenchmark:
    """Fit several classifiers on a shared preprocessing pipeline and collect metrics."""

    def __init__(self, preprocessor_factory):
        self.preprocessor_factory = preprocessor_factory
        self.models = {}
        self.rows = []

    @staticmethod
    def scores(y_true, proba, threshold=0.5):
        pred = (proba >= threshold).astype(int)
        return {
            "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, pred),
            "precision": precision_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
            "recall": recall_score(y_true, pred),
            "f1": f1_score(y_true, pred),
            "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_true, proba),
            "pr_auc": average_precision_score(y_true, proba),
        }

    def fit_evaluate(self, name, estimator, X_tr, y_tr, X_ev, y_ev):
        pipe = Pipeline([("prep", self.preprocessor_factory()), ("model", estimator)])
        pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_ev)[:, 1]
        self.models[name] = pipe
        self.rows.append({"model": name, **self.scores(y_ev, proba)})
        return pipe

    def table(self):
        return pd.DataFrame(self.rows).set_index("model").sort_values("pr_auc", ascending=False)


CANDIDATES = {
    "Dummy (always 0)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=1.0),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=12, min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=SEED),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=2, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED),
    "HistGradientBoosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED),
}
bench = ModelBenchmark(make_preprocessor)
for name, est in CANDIDATES.items():
    bench.fit_evaluate(name, est, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val)
val_table = bench.table()
val_table.round(4)

Finding (figure 4.1). The dummy model reaches 72.4% accuracy but F1 = 0 — proof that accuracy is meaningless here. The two ensembles lead and are almost tied: HistGradientBoosting (F1 0.653, PR-AUC 0.753) and Random Forest (F1 0.646, PR-AUC 0.756). Logistic Regression is last (F1 0.570, PR-AUC 0.684) even with careful scaling → the relationship between features and target is non-linear with interactions (e.g. a long lead time is only risky in some segments). We tune HGB because it trains several times faster than RF.

4.3 Two evaluation traps: target leakage and duplicates¶

Question: if we skipped the cleaning in section 3.1, how artificially good would the scores look?

  • Trap 1 — leakage: keep reservation_status (Canceled/Check-Out/No-Show), reservation_status_date and assigned_room_type.
  • Trap 2 — duplicates: do not remove the 33k duplicated rows before splitting.

Each scenario uses the same default HistGradientBoosting model and the same 70/15/15 split.

In [21]:
def run_scenario(frame, extra_cat=(), extra_num=()):
    X = frame.drop(columns=[target])
    y = frame[target].values
    Xtr, Xtmp, ytr, ytmp = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
    Xv, _, yv, _ = train_test_split(Xtmp, ytmp, test_size=0.50, stratify=ytmp, random_state=SEED)

    def factory():
        base = make_preprocessor()
        cols = base.named_steps["columns"]
        if extra_cat:
            cols.transformers.append(("leak_cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), list(extra_cat)))
        if extra_num:
            cols.transformers.append(("leak_num", "passthrough", list(extra_num)))
        return base

    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", factory()), ("model", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED))]).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    return ModelBenchmark.scores(yv, pipe.predict_proba(Xv)[:, 1])

leaky["status_day_gap"] = (pd.to_datetime(leaky["reservation_status_date"]) -
                           pd.to_datetime(leaky["arrival_date_year"].astype(str) + "-" + leaky["arrival_date_month"] + "-" +
                                          leaky["arrival_date_day_of_month"].astype(str))).dt.days
leaky = leaky.drop(columns=["reservation_status_date"])
leaky = leaky[(leaky["adults"] + leaky["children"].fillna(0) + leaky["babies"] > 0) & leaky["adr"].between(0, 1000)]
leaky = leaky.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

no_dedup = HotelDataCleaner(LEAK_COLS, drop_duplicates=False).clean(raw)

    "With target leakage": run_scenario(leaky, extra_cat=["reservation_status", "assigned_room_type"], extra_num=["status_day_gap"]),
    "Duplicates not removed": run_scenario(no_dedup),

}

Finding (figure 4.3). Keeping the leakage columns yields 1.000 on every metric — the model simply "reads back" the label (reservation_status = Canceled) and would be useless in production. Not removing duplicates pushes F1 from 0.653 to 0.793 (+0.14) and PR-AUC from 0.753 to 0.904 (+0.15): the model memorises copies it saw during training. The honest number is the "Correct process" row — lower, but it reflects how well the model predicts genuinely new bookings.

Separately, hyperparameter tuning raises HGB's validation PR-AUC from 0.753 to 0.768 and F1 from 0.653 to 0.662.

5. Handling class imbalance & choosing a threshold¶

With a 72.4/27.6 split, the default 0.5 threshold may miss many cancellations. We compare three options on the tuned HGB model:

  1. Default — threshold 0.5.
  2. class_weight="balanced" — up-weight the minority class during training.
  3. F1-optimal threshold chosen on the validation set (no retraining).
In [22]:
balanced = clone(tuned).set_params(model__class_weight="balanced").fit(X_train, y_train)
proba_val_bal = balanced.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]

f1s = 2 * prec[:-1] * rec[:-1] / np.clip(prec[:-1] + rec[:-1], 1e-9, None)
best_idx = int(np.nanargmax(f1s))
BEST_THR = float(thr[best_idx])

imb = pd.DataFrame({
    "Default (threshold 0.5)": ModelBenchmark.scores(y_val, proba_val_tuned, 0.5),
    "class_weight=balanced": ModelBenchmark.scores(y_val, proba_val_bal, 0.5),
    f"F1-optimal threshold ({BEST_THR:.2f})": ModelBenchmark.scores(y_val, proba_val_tuned, BEST_THR),
}).T[["precision", "recall", "f1", "pr_auc"]]

Default (threshold 0.5) 0.7207 0.6129 0.6624 0.7676

Finding (figure 5). At the 0.5 threshold the model misses almost 40% of cancellations (recall 0.613). Both remedies trade precision for recall: class_weight=balanced raises recall to 0.814, lowering the threshold to 0.33 raises it to 0.784, and both lift F1 from 0.662 to 0.700. PR-AUC barely moves (0.768) — handling imbalance only shifts the operating point along the same curve; it does not make the model better at ranking. We choose threshold tuning because it reaches the same F1 without retraining, and the threshold can later be adjusted to the hotel's real costs.

6. Final evaluation on the test set¶

In [23]:
FINAL_NAME = "HGB (tuned) + optimal threshold"
final_model = tuned
proba_test = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
pred_test = (proba_test >= BEST_THR).astype(int)
test_scores = ModelBenchmark.scores(y_test, proba_test, BEST_THR)
baseline_lr = bench.models["Logistic Regression"]
lr_test_scores = ModelBenchmark.scores(y_test, baseline_lr.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])

final_tbl = pd.DataFrame({"Logistic Regression (baseline)": lr_test_scores, FINAL_NAME: test_scores}).T
display(final_tbl.round(4))
print(classification_report(y_test, pred_test, target_names=["Not cancelled", "Cancelled"], digits=3))

Test results. The final model reaches F1 0.708, recall 0.786, ROC-AUC 0.898, PR-AUC 0.776 on 12,898 unseen bookings, versus F1 0.580, ROC-AUC 0.853, PR-AUC 0.694 for the Logistic Regression baseline. Test scores match validation (F1 0.700) → choosing the threshold on validation did not overfit. Of the 3,558 real cancellations the model catches 2,795; in exchange 1,542 non-cancelled bookings (16.5%) are flagged by mistake.

6.1 Which features matter most?¶

Permutation importance on the test set: randomly shuffle one original column and measure how much PR-AUC drops. It is computed on columns before preprocessing, so it is easy to interpret (e.g. country covers all of its one-hot columns).

In [25]:
sample_idx = np.random.RandomState(SEED).choice(len(X_test), size=min(6000, len(X_test)), replace=False)
perm = permutation_importance(final_model, X_test.iloc[sample_idx], y_test[sample_idx], scoring="average_precision",
                              n_repeats=5, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
imp = pd.DataFrame({"mean": perm.importances_mean, "std": perm.importances_std}, index=X_test.columns)
imp = imp.sort_values("mean", ascending=False).head(12)

for i, v in enumerate(t["mean"]):
    ax.text(v + t["std"].max() + 0.002, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel("Drop in PR-AUC when the column is shuffled")

Finding (figure 6.1). lead_time (0.147) and country (0.133) matter most, followed by market_segment and total_of_special_requests — consistent with the EDA in section 2.4. Notably, deposit_type only ranks 9th (0.027) even though on the raw data it looked decisive (Non Refund → 99% cancelled): after de-duplication only 1,010 Non Refund bookings remain, so the model no longer relies on it much. Permutation importance measures how much the model relies on a column; it does not prove causation.

6.2 Where does the model fail?¶

Question: is the error rate uniform across market segments?

In [26]:
err = X_test[["market_segment", "hotel"]].copy()
err["y"] = y_test
err["pred"] = pred_test
err["wrong"] = (err["y"] != err["pred"]).astype(int)
seg = err.groupby("market_segment").agg(n=("y", "size"), cancel_rate=("y", "mean"),
                                        error_rate=("wrong", "mean"),
                                        recall=("pred", lambda s: s[err.loc[s.index, "y"] == 1].mean()))
seg = seg[seg["n"] >= 50].sort_values("error_rate", ascending=False)
seg.round(3)

Finding (6.2). Errors concentrate in Online TA (22.6% error rate) — the largest segment with the highest cancellation rate (35.8%) and the most diverse guest behaviour. Conversely, for Direct and Corporate recall is only ~0.41: direct guests rarely cancel (13%), so the model seldom predicts a cancellation for them and misses most of the ones that happen. If the hotel cares about retaining direct guests, a per-segment threshold is worth considering.

Test set Accuracy Precision Recall F1 ROC-AUC PR-AUC
Logistic Regression (baseline) 0.800 0.689 0.501 0.580 0.853 0.694
HGB tuned + threshold 0.33 0.821 0.645 0.786 0.708 0.898 0.776
  1. Cleaning determines whether the results can be trusted. 27.8% of the rows are duplicates and 3 columns leak the target; ignoring them gives "great" F1 scores of 0.79–1.00 that are simply wrong. After cleaning, the true cancellation rate is 27.6% (not 37%).
  2. Non-linear ensembles work best. Tuned HistGradientBoosting beats Logistic Regression by +0.13 F1 and +0.08 PR-AUC on the test set.
  3. The threshold matters as much as the model. Lowering it from 0.5 to 0.33 raises recall from 0.61 to 0.78 — catching roughly one extra cancellation in six.
  4. Strongest signals: booking far in advance (long lead time), nationality, sales channel, and the guest making no special requests.

Limitations.

  • Random rather than time-based split: in production the model must predict future bookings, so real-world scores may be lower.
  • Data from only two hotels in Portugal, 2015–2017 (pre-COVID) — today's cancellation behaviour may differ.
  • The threshold is optimised for F1, which assumes a missed cancellation and a false alarm cost the same.

Future work. Time-based split (train 2015–2016, test 2017); choose the threshold from real business costs; TargetEncoder for high-cardinality country/agent; probability calibration so scores can drive overbooking directly; per-prediction explanations with SHAP.
